crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Self-Driving Laboratories
children.blurb: A self-driving laboratory is a closed-loop experimental system in which an artificial intelligence agent selects experiments, robotic hardware performs them, and analytical instruments feed results back to the agent.

children.name: Digital Twins for Experiments
children.blurb: A digital twin for an experiment is a live computational model of a physical laboratory setup, its instruments, samples, and protocols, used to plan, monitor, and interpret runs.

children.name: Instrument and Sensor Data
children.blurb: Instrument and sensor data in laboratory automation and simulation covers the raw and processed signals from analytical instruments, environmental sensors, imaging systems, and robotic lab equipment.

children.name: Optimising Lab Protocols
children.blurb: Optimising lab protocols uses AI and simulation to refine the sequence, timing, and parameters of experimental procedures.

children.name: Forecasting Lab Supplies
children.blurb: Forecasting lab supplies means predicting future demand for consumables, reagents, equipment parts, and other inventory in research and clinical laboratories.

sections.body: Laboratory automation and simulation covers the use of artificial intelligence to run physical experiments, model them before they happen, and manage the resources they consume. In practice, AI systems now control liquid handling robots, choose which experiments to run next, and adjust conditions such as temperature or reagent volume without a person at the bench. Digital twins simulate a reaction or instrument state so researchers can test changes cheaply before committing materials. Instrument and sensor data is parsed in real time to flag anomalies, calibrate readings, and turn raw output into structured results. Protocol optimisation uses machine learning to search over parameters like mixing time or pH, while supply forecasting predicts when consumables will run low based on past usage.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Parsing instrument data and optimising well defined protocols are the most mature areas, with reliable results for assays that have large, clean datasets. Self-driving laboratories can run closed loops for narrow tasks, such as finding a better solvent ratio, but they still struggle when the search space is large or the goal is poorly specified. Digital twins are useful for simple physical systems, yet they often fail to capture the complexity of living cells or multi step reactions. Supply forecasting works well for stable, high volume items but degrades when suppliers change, experiments shift, or demand is sporadic. Across the 135 research papers in this site's library, the honest limit is that most demonstrations are small scale and tied to a single lab's equipment.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader would start with Instrument and Sensor Data to understand how raw signals become usable measurements, because every other page depends on that foundation. Digital Twins for Experiments then shows how those measurements can build a simulation that predicts outcomes before physical work begins. Self-Driving Laboratories sits on top of both, using the data and the model to choose and run the next experiment automatically. Optimising Lab Protocols is the practical application of that loop, focused on finding better parameters for a specific assay or process. Forecasting Lab Supplies is the operational side, using usage patterns from instrument logs and experiment schedules to keep the lab stocked. Together the pages move from sensing, to simulating, to acting, and finally to resourcing.
